captions.text: On your shared screen now: the “Projectile Motion” derivation notes. It sets up the uncoupled equations, m x double dot equals zero, m y double dot equals minus m g, with initial velocities v zero cos theta and v zero sin theta. Then it integrates to give x of t and y of t, leading toward the trajectory. Where would you like to focus?
I don't see a box on your shared screen, Vivek Bot. Maybe start with the uncoupled equations mx double dot equals zero and...
Okay, yes, those. We have m...
Vivek Bot, can you tell me why the horizontal acceleration is zero in equation one?

Yes. Because in our model, gravity acts only vertically, and we’re neglecting air resistance. So, no horizontal force means no horizontal acceleration m x double dot equals zero. That’s just Newton’s second law in the x-direction.
So, what would it take to make it non-zero?
You’d need some horizontal force. Like air drag, or maybe thrust if it’s powered. Then m x double dot wouldn’t be zero.
Yeah, the notes say the two directions are uncoupled. What does that actually mean in this context?

Right. It means the x motion and the y motion don’t affect each other. Each obeys its own equation. You can solve for x of t without knowing y, and solve for y of t without knowing x, and only at the end do you combine them, for example to get the trajectory.
But would that still hold once you include air resistance?
Not usually. With air resistance, the force often depends on the speed or direction of motion, which mixes x and y. Then the equations become coupled and you can’t solve them fully independently.
Could you read me the initial conditions and equation five out loud, please?
Sure. The initial conditions are x of zero equals zero, y of zero equals zero, x dot of zero equals v zero cos theta, and y dot of zero equals v zero sin theta.
Mm-hmm. And equation five?
So why does that make the path a parabola, though? Why not some other kind of curve?
Equation five is the vertical position: y of t equals v zero
Mm, good question. Let me walk that through.
Because when you eliminate time between x of t and y of t, y becomes a constant times x minus a constant times x squared. That’s a quadratic in x, and any quadratic graphs as a parabola.
What do your notes give for the maximum height, and what's its equation number?
S-
Sure. Checking that now.

My shared screen only shows up through equation five for y of t. I’ll move to the next part of the notes so we can see the maximum height. Okay, it’s here. They set y dot to zero, find the peak at t star equals v zero sin theta over g, and the maximum height is...
Hey, where does that time of flight come from? Can you walk me through it?
Sure. Time of flight comes from setting y equal to zero again and solving for T. That gives T equals two v zero sin theta over g, labeled as equation seven.
And what's the solution for when T equals zero?
Hmm, I can’t actually read the shared notes from here, so I can’t confirm the exact maximum I’ve just drawn a box around: v zero sin theta T minus one half g T squared equals zero,
And the one where t equals zero? What's that solution?
That’s the launch instant.
The other solution gives the landing time: T equals two v zero sin theta over g, which is equation seven, and
Don't read it out to me again. Just tell me why the time of flight is two v naught sine theta over g.
That’s the launch instant. The nonzero one is the actual flight time, T equals two v zero sin theta over g.
